The prospect of animation studios releasing "real-time" versions of their CGI animated movies, where visuals are rendered in real-time on a computer or game console's GPU, is a tantalizing one. However, this approach would necessitate a plethora of challenges, which would likely hinder the studios' success.

Firstly, the technical requirements for rendering high-quality, photorealistic visuals in real-time are substantial. The graphics processing unit (GPU) would need to be extremely powerful, with a high number of cores and a robust memory bandwidth. This would necessitate significant investments in hardware and software, which could be a considerable financial burden for studios.

Furthermore, the computational resources required to render complex scenes in real-time would be substantial. The GPU would need to be able to handle a large number of concurrent threads, each responsible for rendering a specific aspect of the scene. This would require significant optimization of the rendering pipeline, as well as the development of new algorithms and techniques to efficiently manage the computational load.

Another significant challenge would be the need for a robust and efficient rendering engine. The engine would need to be able to handle a wide range of visual effects, including lighting, shading, and texturing, all while maintaining a high frame rate. This would require significant expertise in computer graphics, as well as a deep understanding of the underlying physics and mathematics.

Additionally, the real-time rendering approach would require significant changes to the animation production pipeline. The studios would need to adopt new workflows and tools, which would require significant training and investment in new software and hardware. This could be a significant barrier to entry for studios that are not already familiar with real-time rendering technologies.

Furthermore, the real-time rendering approach would also require significant changes to the animation production process. The studios would need to adopt a more iterative and flexible approach to animation, with a focus on creating a cohesive and engaging narrative. This would require significant changes to the way that animators work, as well as the development of new tools and techniques to facilitate real-time collaboration and feedback.

In terms of the business model, the real-time rendering approach would likely require significant changes to the way that studios distribute and monetize their content. The studios would need to adopt new distribution models, such as streaming or cloud-based services, which would require significant investments in infrastructure and logistics.

Finally, the real-time rendering approach would also require significant changes to the way that studios market and promote their content. The studios would need to adopt new marketing strategies, which would require significant investments in social media, advertising, and other promotional channels.

In conclusion, while the idea of releasing real-time versions of CGI animated movies is an intriguing one, it is unlikely that animation studios would be successful in this approach. The technical, financial, and logistical challenges are significant, and would require significant investments in hardware, software, and personnel. However, the potential rewards of real-time rendering are substantial, and it is likely that we will see significant advancements in this area in the coming years.
